A disease name is annotated as **Modifier** when it functions as a noun modifier of a non-disease head, such as a protein, gene, family, phenotype, cohort, population, case series, or kindred.

If the disease term is *directly* followed by a head noun, with no preposition, article, determiner, parenthesis, or participial clause between them, it is a pre-nominal adjunct and is labeled **Modifier**.

**Label as Disease Class** when a span denotes a pathological state, clinical sign, or deficiency without a fixed disease name, either because its head noun is a state, sign, abnormality, or deficiency noun, or because a deviation qualifier (such as “abnormal,” “deficient,” or “defective”) modifies a process or substance noun, **and** the span is linked to a named disorder through a characterization, causal, or consequence frame (e.g., “is characterized by,” “is caused by,” “results in,” “secondary to”).

quotes.quote: Non-disease heads linked to a named disorder, and feature terms in definitional descriptions, are Disease Class. A patient-level role does not promote them to Specific Disease.
A disease name is annotated as **Modifier** when it functions as a noun modifier of a non-disease head, such as a protein, gene, family, phenotype, cohort, population, case series, or kindred.

If the disease term is *directly* followed by a head noun, with no preposition, article, determiner, parenthesis, or participial clause between them, it is a pre-nominal adjunct and is labeled **Modifier**.

If the disease term is not a pre-nominal adjunct, and it is (a) the complement of a preposition, (b) introduced by an article or determiner, or (c) a parenthetical acronym or abbreviation of the disease itself, it is labeled **Specific Disease** (referential mention).
**Label as Specific Disease** when the phrase is anchored to one individuated condition, either: - by a proper name, eponym, acronym, gene, or pathogen identity

If the disease term is not a pre-nominal adjunct, and it is (a) the complement of a preposition, (b) introduced by an article or determiner, or (c) a parenthetical acronym or abbreviation of the disease itself, it is labeled **Specific Disease** (referential mention).

**Label as Disease Class** when: - the phrase is a superordinate category reference that enumerates or classifies kinds of disease (introduced by “such as,” “including,” “types of,” or a class-membership frame, e.g., “is an autosomal recessive disease”)

quotes.quote: **Label as Disease Class** when: - the phrase is a superordinate category reference that enumerates or classifies kinds of disease (introduced by “such as,” “including,” “types of,” or a class-membership frame, e.g., “is an autosomal recessive disease”); or - the phrase is a phenotype or feature term listed in a generic, definitional description of a syndrome or entity, rather than a condition that a specific individual has or is diagnosed with (e.g., “mental retardation” in “…is characterized by ichthyosis, mental retardation, and spasticity”).
quotes.condition_words: a phenotype or feature term listed in a generic, definitional description

A disease named in a family history of relatives, or used to describe a cohort or case series, is a **Modifier** when it names one disease.
quotes.condition_words: used to describe a cohort or case series

quotes.quote: **Family-history and cohort descriptors** are **Modifier** (Section 3), even when the disease term is the complement of “of” (e.g., “a family history of ovarian cancer”).

If the disease term is *directly* followed by a head noun, with no preposition, article, determiner, parenthesis, or participial clause between them, it is a pre-nominal adjunct and is labeled **Modifier**.

A contiguous span in which a coordinator (e.g., “or,” “and,” “and/or,” a slash, “nor”) joins two or more disease terms is one **Composite Mention** when a conjunct depends on the shared head or modifier for its disease identity. This includes elliptical forms in which the head noun appears only once after the last conjunct (e.g., “breast or ovarian cancer”; “colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers”). The rule holds in any syntactic slot: prenominal, prepositional complement, or attributive before a non-disease head such as a relational noun phrase (“family history”), a population, a case series, or a study noun. A span is a **Modifier** only when it contains exactly one disease concept.

A coordinated span in which a conjunct depends on the shared disease head, or in which the conjuncts are disease concepts that cannot be split without loss, is one Composite Mention in any syntactic slot, including family-history and cohort descriptors.

The rule holds in any syntactic slot: prenominal, prepositional complement, or attributive before a non-disease head such as a relational noun phrase (“family history”), a population, a case series, or a study noun.

A coordinated span in which a conjunct depends on the shared disease head, or in which the conjuncts are disease concepts that cannot be split without loss, is one Composite Mention in any syntactic slot, including family-history and cohort descriptors.

Do NOT trim when the full span is an established, fixed name, including: - an eponym followed by a disease-type head noun, even with internal modifiers (e.g., “Sjogren-Larsson syndrome,” “Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome,” “Coats disease”); - a head-final compound whose non-head element is an identifier or proper name (e.g., “Coats telangiectasis,” “G6PD deficiency”); - a subtype or inheritance term that is part of a recognized concept or established name
quotes.condition_words: a subtype or inheritance term that is part of a recognized concept or established name
